props.title: Doom
props.initialSlug: Space Marines battle demons on Mars research base

sections.content: **Doom** (2005) represents both the challenges and occasional successes of video game adaptations. Following in the footsteps of **Resident Evil** (2002), it attempted to translate first-person shooter mechanics to film, most notably in its innovative FPS sequence near the climax. While the film struggled critically, it sits alongside other early-2000s game adaptations like **House of the Dead** (2003) and **Alone in the Dark** (2005) as examples of Hollywood trying to crack the video game code, albeit with mixed results.

sections.content: The Rock's performance as Sarge in **Doom** (2005) came during his early transition from wrestling to acting, alongside other action roles like **The Rundown** (2003) and **Walking Tall** (2004). Karl Urban's role as Reaper preceded his later sci-fi work in **Dredd** (2012) and **Star Trek** (2009), showing his capability in the genre. The film's practical effects and monster designs by Stan Winston Studios follow a tradition of practical creature features like **Dog Soldiers** (2002) and **Pitch Black** (2000).

The film's Mars setting connects it to a larger tradition of Mars-based sci-fi horror, from **Total Recall** (1990) to **Ghosts of Mars** (2001) and later **Red Planet** (2000). Its confined corridor shooting and monster reveals draw from classics like **Aliens** (1986), while its genetic mutation plot points echo **Resident Evil** (2002) and **Species** (1995). sections.content: **Doom** (2005) arrived during a transitional period for game adaptations. While earlier attempts like **Super Mario Bros.** (1993) took massive liberties with source material, **Doom** tried to maintain core game elements while building a more conventional narrative. This approach influenced later adaptations like **Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time** (2010) and **Assassin's Creed** (2016), though the real breakthrough wouldn't come until **Detective Pikachu** (2019) and **Sonic the Hedgehog** (2020).
